title: I ported my Three.js rally game to Godot, got it running great... and decided to stick with Three.js anyway
author: Conscious-Desk6823
selftext:
Hey everyone!

First of all, a big thank you to everyone who responded to my previous post! I honestly didn't expect so much advice, feedback, and encouragement. 🙏

One of the biggest discussions was whether I should move to Godot or keep building on my custom Three.js setup. I actually explored both directions and ended up leaning toward the latter. So here's a little update, along with some before-and-after images.

For those who missed it: I'm an art director, not a developer. What started as a simple 2D canvas experiment with Claude has slowly turned into **Over The Edge**, an isometric rally game built with Three.js. Inspired by classic Colin McRae, but focused more on arcade fun, ridiculous corners, and pushing friends off cliffs.

**So, about that Godot port...**  
Following some of your suggestions, I decided to give Godot a proper try. Surprisingly, it went really well. I built a way to export the generated stages into Godot, and before long, most of the game was running there.

But maintaining two versions quickly became a headache. Meanwhile, I also followed the advice to keep improving the custom Three.js engine, and many of the performance issues turned out to be fixable.  


https://i.redd.it/ueu1tkixm82i1.png

**The biggest performance improvement actually came from rethinking anti-aliasing.** Instead of relying on how Three.js was handling it, I experimented with a custom approach that turned out to be much more efficient for this particular game. It made a surprisingly big difference to how smoothly everything runs. I only discovered this thanks to **Fable 5.2**. and continuous tries to optimize. 

So for now, I'm sticking with Three.js. Not because Godot didn't work, but because improving what I already had made more sense. And being able to share the game instantly through a browser is still a huge advantage. Plus I didn't feel like the performance took a giant leap compared to Three.js  


https://i.redd.it/firxeu2in82i1.png

**The cars are still generated through code but different.**  
Multiple people asked me how assets are made. (cars in this case) I've started using ChatGPT to generate blueprints based on real rally cars, then direct Claude to turn those references into 3D geometry using JavaScript. Before this method I had an example car and moved from there to generate more cars. The new way still isn't one-shotting cars through the pipeline.

There's a lot of comparing proportions, tweaking details, and iterating. Some cars still look questionable, but the newer ones are actually more detailed while using fewer polygons. Claude really doesnt like clean 3d models it seems. But it's slowly learning how to better itself based on past iterations. 😄



![img](9p2ggfp4n82i1 "The cars became a lot more smooth and complex while at the same time lost 60% of the polygons. (cars now sit around 15k polygons)")

  
**Procedural stages need a human touch**  
Just letting AI generate roads and environments doesn't necessarily result in something fun to drive.

I've directed Claude to build a system using building blocks I've designed, like different corners, elevation changes, villages, and obstacles.



![img](wukmbcspm82i1 "I've let Claude create a stage editor to easily check what it generates")

The endless mode generates new stages live using those blocks. But the regular stages still require lots of manual tweaking and testing to get the flow right.

A stage can look great from above and be absolutely terrible to drive.



![img](gyt9pxb1n82i1 "@taisui asked me why I limited the camera angle to an isometric perspective. I tried to do it different. But I havent felt more nauseous in my life. Looks pretty though.")

**Making the world feel more alive**  
I've connected ElevenLabs to create a co-driver who calls out pace notes and occasionally comments when you crash. That worked way better than I expected. I took a lot of inspiration from the Colin McRae series regarding the voice.

The rest of the soundscape was a combination between Claude generating basic audio and some sounds from an online Folio platform. So this has improved quite a bit, with cheering crowds, wind, gravel, dirt rubbing against the car, and the first proper crash and scrape sounds.

  


![img](ywjk3znqn82i1 "I use claude to compare different styles. And then review them first before making a decision.")

**The biggest thing I've learned**  
Even though Claude does all the coding, I've spent a ridiculous amount of time directing everything.

Testing, tweaking, providing references, reshaping systems, and making sure things actually look and feel right.

As an art director, it's a familiar process, but AI can build something incredibly quickly without necessarily understanding what makes it *good*.

The procedural stages are probably the best example. Generating a road is easy. Making one that's genuinely fun to drive takes a lot more thought.

It's still pretty wonky and far from finished, but I'm happy with how much has changed.

For the people asking how much time this has taken. Ive tracked every minute of it. 😅



https://i.redd.it/d8ur7j19n82i1.png

**I'm curious if others working on bigger AI-assisted projects have experienced the same thing. Does AI actually save you time, or do you end up spending that time directing and refining instead?**

Thanks again for all the feedback last time. It really has helped! For anyone curious to try the current version, it's playable directly in your browser:

[https://overtheedge.app](https://overtheedge.app/)

Still very much a work in progress, so feedback is always welcome. Especially curious how it runs on different machines!

Long post sorry!

comments.author: EmergencyShutdown
comments.body:
I loved the first iteration - and you've only made it better. Nice work.  And I agree - you can't beat javascript in terms of rapid build, test, and sharing. Everytime I experiement with something else - I always end up back at three.js as well. 

a few notes -   
first - the sense of speed is a bit off - it feels slow - but at the same time, increadibly difficult - going faster would require trade-offs in course design.   
  
second - personally - i do not like the isometric fixed view - I'd much rather have some sort of chase cam - even if it's locked to the course position, not the necessarily the car.   
  
third - I haven't had time to really test a lot of levels in this game yet - but on a real rally stage - going straight, fast, is hard - the ground is not flat, smooth, or forgiving --- keeping the car balanced when the left side is getting slightly different traction than the right side, when the road has subtle camber or crown variations .. etc.. -- that really differentiates "real" rallly from a lot of arcade style sims.  (not saying your doing this wrong - just something speaking from my own personal experience - someone who competed in Rally America years ago - and have since decided to make my own rally inspired games) 

I'll keep playing it and maybe have some better feedback at some point..  But  - good job on this so far,

replies.author: Conscious-Desk6823
replies.body: Love this feedback! Thank you. I will play around with the feeling of speed and camera settings. Still on the fence how to make the camera more dynamic. I know it needs a bit of getting use to.

replies.author: EmergencyShutdown
replies.body: Playing with an Xbox controller - the vibration feedback is a bit overwhelming - really needs to be dialed back some.

replies.author: Conscious-Desk6823
replies.body: Oh man thats good to know. Only have a ps5 controller myself. Ill put it on the list right away. 🙌

replies.author: EmergencyShutdown
replies.body:
One other thing - the car points \_exactly\_ where you steer -  you still slide - traction isn't direct - but the car rotates instantly. You don't get a good feel of how the car is oversteering, and you can't slide and countersteer out of a turn.   
Probably fine for an arcade game - but being able to nail a Scandinavian flick out in a hairpin is the quintessential rally maneuver.

replies.author: Conscious-Desk6823
replies.body: I agree fully. Did you create an account? Maybe i can give you access to the “real” steering option. I need to develop this further but I could use your vision.

replies.author: EmergencyShutdown
replies.body: Not yet but i certainly would be willing to

replies.author: Conscious-Desk6823
replies.body: Dm me when you do. I can give you access to some features and stages ive been playing with.

replies.author: EmergencyShutdown
replies.body:
My last criticism for now --- (And don't get me wrong - I'm loving playing this so far) -- so genuinely I hope you are taking this as constructive feedback - not a bashing the work you've done... 

  
Each level is "unique" -- but the progression through each biome is so rapid fire - no single level has a distinctive character. Each level is just a mess of rapid fire turns and surfaces.  Right now it's \~100 meters of gravel, followed by 100 meters of asphalt, into a courtyard, immediately into 100 meters of sand.. 

I'd suggest extending each biome out 4 or 5x the current distance so that each level only has 2 or 3 total. This way - the player can get into a rhythm - and - ideally - each new level spawns with a distinctive, new feel... 

After \~5 levels I am already starting to feel like I've seen everything the maps have to offer (i'm sure i haven't) -- but it's the same features over and over.   
  
i want a distinctive level that feel's like it has purpose - not a random assault of everything you have plus the kitchen sink.

replies.author: Conscious-Desk6823
replies.body: No dont worry! I love the detailed feedback. It will only make it better in the end. I’m also fan of longer more dedicated stages. But playing with some friends they felt the longer stages 1400m quite “long”. So i kept them shorter for now. Actually the USA and Bolivia have a stronger thematic progression. Which I want to work back into spain and sweden. So good that you pointed this out. And I will pick this up sooner than later.

comments.author: HockeyDadNinja
comments.body:
This is awesome and fun! I love the arcade feel and it reminds me of Super Sprint.

I'm building a kind of console arcade for web games like this that runs in any browser that I'm running in Android TV. I just played it on my Nvidia Shield TV but the graphics were degraded and the sound was choppy.

The page sends any Android user agent to the mobile page, so Android TV gets "play this on a computer". I had to send a desktop user agent to get in. A check for a touch screen, or a URL flag to skip the redirect, would let TV boxes through.

The menus read only the first connected gamepad. On the Shield my kb/mouse USB receiver shows up as gamepad 0 with no standard mapping, so the real controller (gamepad 1) could not press Next or drive. It worked after I unplugged the receiver. Skipping pads that don't have the standard mapping would fix it.

\- The sound was choppy and the graphics looked degraded the whole time, even in quiet parts.  
\- Device: Shield TV 2019 (Tegra X1+), Android System WebView 157, WebGL2  
\- Median FPS: 29.9 over a 148 second session  
\- 1% low FPS: 1.1, so there are long stalls  
\- Peak memory of the page renderer: 537 MB

The Shield is fast for an Android TV box, so a Chromecast or Google TV Streamer will be slower. If you want a hand getting it running well on a device like this let me know. It would be a cool addition to my arcade app and the problem so far has been finding console friendly games like this.

comments.author: dotoonly
comments.body:
The fix on threejs definitely can be applied to godot. You just need to tell AI to create the workflow to build a custom godot engine. This way it can access and change renderer code just like how it does with threejs. It can even compare bit by bit change between the two version.  
Going with godot can help you later on many issues that might take significant effort or token such as stable physics behavior (most important), custom input swaping (controller, steering wheel, etc). These are the fundamental features that any racing game should have.

comments.author: Russ_72days
comments.body:
Given you can only steer left and right I wonder if a “slide” system for steering would be an interesting option. If I place my thumb anywhere on left hand side it picks that up as the central steering point. Then if I slide to the left or right from there it controls the amount of turn. If you lift your thumb it centres again. For a game that’s mostly about sliding around, it felt like it might be a more natural fit than a lots little taps. That said - could be a terrible idea in practice!!

Also, if you are planning on selling the game in App and Play Store - Godot would be a more slicker native experience than wrapping ThreeJS app in capacitor or equivalent(I would assume) tho I’m sure Claude can give you a more qualified opinion there

comments.author: Free-Spirit-8327
comments.body:
I love racing games. Played since I was a kid, and usually put them on the most difficult settings. So I have one feedback for this game.

The car needs more traction. As it is, to turn, you pretty much have to be somewhere between 45-90 degrees turned to get any meaningful turning with the car. I think this is bad, because a lot of the driving ends up being about whether of not you're fast enough to turn the car around to the other side. If you get it to turn a bit too much in a corner, it's extremely unforgiving because you have to turn the car to the other side to correct it. It's like driving on ice. On straights, you can pretty much swing the car left and right 45 degrees both directions without actually changing driving direction.

Useful feedback! The understeer your describing depends partly on the drivetrain of the car you're driving + the arcade steering. Im going to work on a realistic steering that maybe gives what you're looking for.

For example the weekly that's now active has a RWD car.
